stories.title: AI Proves Signal's Encryption Correct, Down to the Machine Code
stories.story:
For decades, formal verification — mathematically proving that software does exactly what it claims — has been the gold standard of security assurance and also, almost always, impractical. Expert teams spending years on a single protocol, verifying only small scopes of code, was the norm. The gap between what was provably safe and what billions of people actually used remained wide open.

On November 10, Google DeepMind announced it had closed a meaningful piece of that gap. Its new agentic framework, AlphaProof Code, used teams of AI agents powered by the Gemini model to formally verify key security properties of Signal's cryptographic protocol — not the design document, but the actual compiled AArch64 binary that runs on devices. Five researchers guided the process over four weeks, a task that historically takes expert teams years. The agents generated roughly 6.5 million lines of machine-checked Lean proof code, resting on about 26,000 lines of human-written specifications.

Two claims stand out. First, it is the first formal verification of a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth by any method. Second, the system also correctly identified known bugs when researchers reintroduced two previously fixed flaws into Signal's code, suggesting it can tell the difference between correct and broken — a crucial sanity check. The same protocol underpins encrypted messages in WhatsApp and Google Messages, meaning the security envelope covers far more than Signal's own users.

DeepMind open-sourced the verification artifacts and published a technical paper alongside the announcement. The next implication is structural: if verification agents can be embedded in ordinary software development pipelines, the asymmetry that has always favored attackers — they need to find one flaw; defenders must seal every one — could start to shift.
stories.hook: We've always assumed software has bugs we just haven't found yet — this is the first serious attempt to mathematically prove otherwise, on code people actually use.

stories.title: Anthropic Takes AI's Largest IPO to Wall Street
stories.story:
In 2013, Dario Amodei was a researcher at OpenAI. By 2021, convinced that frontier AI needed more rigorous safety work than a startup racing for revenue could deliver, he and several colleagues walked out and founded Anthropic as a Public Benefit Corporation — a legal structure meant to subordinate profit to mission. That constitutional choice is now being stress-tested in the most public way imaginable.

On November 10, Anthropic launched its IPO roadshow, offering 825 million Class A shares at a proposed price of $70 to $78 each, targeting a raise of up to roughly $64 billion. A listing on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT is expected as early as November 19–20. The numbers dwarf every prior technology offering in history. What makes them stranger is the tension embedded in the filing itself: last quarter Anthropic logged $17 billion in revenue and a $536 million operating loss. Goldman Sachs, one of the lead underwriters, reportedly projects the company will close the year at around $52 billion in annualized revenue — roughly seven times what it earned in all of 2025.

The structural novelty runs deeper than the PBC label. Seven of Anthropic's largest suppliers — AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC — have committed to buying $26 billion worth of shares through a private placement alongside the public offering. The chip industry is essentially co-signing the company's balance sheet, binding its own fortunes to Anthropic's survival. That is less an IPO than a managed syndication of the AI supply chain.

The implication is uncomfortable: a company founded explicitly to slow down and scrutinize powerful AI is now racing to list at a valuation that demands perpetual scale. Public markets do not reward caution; they reward growth. The roadshow is where Anthropic's founding paradox goes to get priced.
stories.hook: They left OpenAI to build AI more carefully — and are now executing the largest tech IPO in history to fund it.

stories.title: Inflation's Ghost Reappears, and the Fed Faces a Familiar Corner
stories.story:
For three consecutive months, core consumer prices in the United States have risen 0.3 percent — each time, a tenth of a percentage point above what forecasters expected. October's reading, released Tuesday, was no exception. Headline CPI came in at 0.4 percent month-on-month, shelter costs climbed again, and food posted its largest monthly gain since April. The year-over-year rate was not published at all: a government shutdown in late 2025 left the Bureau of Labor Statistics without October 2025 price data to compare against, an absence that is itself a symptom of the dysfunction surrounding this inflation fight.

The mechanics here matter. Hours before the data dropped, Fed Governor Christopher Waller told a Bank of England conference in London that if core inflation hit 0.3 percent or higher, a 50-basis-point December hike should be on the table — twice the standard move. The data obliged. By Tuesday's close, markets had fully priced in a December hike, with roughly 15 percent odds on the larger half-point increase. The 2-year Treasury yield surged 13 basis points in a single session. The S&P 500 fell, the Nasdaq dropped 0.74 percent, and the dollar rallied sharply.

What makes this consequential is the feedback loop it has restarted. The Fed paused in October — its benchmark rate sitting at 3.75 to 4 percent — after three years of hikes that were supposed to have broken inflation's back. Now market-implied odds of a January hike have jumped from roughly 20 percent to over 60 percent in a single day. Three consecutive sticky core readings, analysts note, suggest the problem is not energy or supply-chain echoes but durable demand — shelter, services, food. If that is true, the Fed's December decision is not a question of 25 versus 50 basis points. It is a question of whether this cycle ever actually ended.
stories.hook: The Fed declared victory on inflation, then inflation sent back a memo.
stories.source: ING Think / BLS CPI Release, November 10, 2026

stories.title: CoreWeave's Earnings Beat Cannot Outrun Its Debt Machine
stories.story:
CoreWeave reported Q3 revenue up 168% year-over-year — a number that would make most companies euphoric. And yet the market barely exhaled. That is because the company's story has stopped being about growth and started being about arithmetic.

The AI neocloud, which leases high-performance GPU clusters to companies training and running large language models, has built its empire almost entirely on borrowed money. It entered the third quarter carrying nearly $47 billion in total debt — against a business that has never turned a profit. When the Federal Reserve began signaling aggressive rate hikes after October's hotter-than-expected inflation print, that debt load went from uncomfortable to alarming. Bond investors responded by pushing yields on CoreWeave's 2031 notes above 16%, a level associated with distressed credit, not a growth darling.

The mechanics are almost classical. CoreWeave borrows to buy Nvidia chips and build data centers. Those assets take time to generate revenue. Meanwhile, rising rates make each new dollar of debt more expensive. If lenders lose confidence and withdraw, the company cannot fund new capacity. Without new capacity, contracted backlog — $132.5 billion as of September — becomes impossible to deliver. And if delivery slips, customers pull commitments, which makes lenders even less willing to extend credit. CEO Mike Intrator called it plainly: "a doom cycle."

This week's earnings provided a temporary reprieve. Management disclosed $9 billion in customer prepayments arriving within three months and vowed to avoid unsecured parent-level debt at current yields. But with the Fed now openly debating a half-point hike in December, the cost of capital for every debt-funded AI infrastructure company will keep climbing. CoreWeave is the most visible stress point, but it is not alone — IREN carries $10 billion in debt, and Bank of America estimates AI-related credit issuance will hit $685 billion next year.
stories.hook: The AI boom was always a capital story; now the capital is getting expensive.

stories.title: Twenty-One Banks Pool $270 Million to Challenge Tether and Circle
stories.story:
For a decade, the stablecoin market worked like a tollbooth that banks built the road to but never owned. Tether and Circle collected the fees. That arrangement may now be ending.

A consortium of 21 financial institutions — including Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Bank of America, Deutsche Bank, Wells Fargo, UBS, and MUFG — has formally committed roughly $270 million to a joint stablecoin venture codenamed Project Faro. The capital covers five years of operations for a U.S.-incorporated entity. The plan is to launch a dollar-denominated token in the first half of 2027, with euro and other G7-currency versions to follow. The consortium is still searching for a chief executive and has not settled on a final company name.

The mechanism matters more than the headline number. Banks already manage the treasury services, cross-border payments, and institutional custody relationships that any stablecoin needs to become useful at scale. Project Faro is essentially a bid to convert those existing pipes into on-chain distribution — bypassing the customer-acquisition problem that slowed every crypto-native entrant. When the consortium's plan first leaked in September, Circle's stock fell roughly 6 percent in a single session.

The structural wrinkle is that several Faro members are simultaneously backing rivals. BBVA is in both Faro and Open USD, a Stripe-led effort that includes Visa. Rabobank belongs to Faro and to Qivalis, the European consortium that just received electronic money institution authorization from the Dutch central bank in October. The hedging signals genuine uncertainty about which architecture wins — not disloyalty to Faro. What it confirms is that traditional finance has collectively decided the stablecoin layer of global payments is too important to cede to anyone else.
stories.hook: The banks didn't miss crypto — they just waited until they could arrive with $270 billion in existing customer relationships instead of a whitepaper.
